turns.en: Life to a mundane question, but I feel like we should ask this. But what does your token spend look like now versus, say, last year or in 2023?
turns.zh: 转到一个平凡的问题，但我觉得我们应该问这个。你们现在的 token 花费，跟比如去年、或者 2023 年相比，是什么样子？

turns.en: It's up like 200x or so. So extremely fast and paying off. We're managing a significant investment management fund. So our AI is profitable.
turns.zh: 涨了大约 200 倍。所以极其快，而且有回报。我们管理着一只规模可观的投资管理基金。所以我们的 AI 是盈利的。

turns.en: How do you judge whether it's paying off?
turns.zh: 你怎么判断它有没有回报？

turns.en: Well, that's what I'm saying. For us, we have a fund in which we make fixed fees and performance fees. We have a value-creating AI that's generating more value than we're paying it. And one of the ways we set it up is as it makes money, we put more into making the intelligence better, which when you think about companies, say we're on a better track than what we were just talking about, that that's the way I think you'll see this disruption in industry scale, right? That the people that can use intelligence... that generate revenue that could then put that revenue back into generating better intelligence can create this moat. And so when you think about Bridgewater, that's what we're trying to design is this moat where, okay, we're getting better and better intelligence about how to predict what's next in the world. That intelligence by predicting what's next in the world can generate money that can generate the flywheel to, okay, now we got more money to generate a smarter intelligence. And that's the path that we're on. That's how we can measure whether our investments are paying off. Is it actually successfully predicting? what's next in the world.
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是我要说的。对我们而言，我们有一只基金，从中收取固定费用（fixed fees）和业绩报酬（performance fees）。我们有一个创造价值的 AI，它产生的价值超过了我们为它付出的成本。我们搭建它的方式之一是：当它赚钱时，我们就把更多投入用于让智能变得更好。想想公司吧，比如说我们处在一条比刚才谈的更好的轨道上——我认为你将会在行业规模上看到这种颠覆，对吧？那些能使用智能……能产生营收、进而把营收回投到生成更好智能的人，能构筑起这条护城河（moat）。所以当你想到 Bridgewater，我们试图设计的正是这条护城河：好，我们正在获得越来越好的智能，去预测世界接下来会发生什么。而这种智能通过预测世界接下来会发生什么，能产生钱，进而形成飞轮（flywheel）：好，现在我们有了更多钱去生成更聪明的智能。这就是我们所走的道路。这也是我们衡量自己的投资有没有回报的方式——它是否真的在成功地预测世界接下来会发生什么。

turns.en: What's your constraint? You know, like everyone, if we're just going back to the world of markets, everyone wants to know what the bottleneck is. If you could snap your fingers, what thing would you like to have more of right now that would solve problems?
turns.zh: 你的约束是什么？你知道，就像每个人——如果我们回到市场的世界——每个人都想知道瓶颈在哪里。如果你能打个响指，你现在最希望多拥有什么东西，来解决这些问题？

turns.en: Yeah, I'd say, interestingly, that the human constraint that has been tough is, and really powerful when it works, is this scientist-investor collaboration. So really getting scientists to be practical enough to see actually what the game is when you're investing, right? Investing is a really interesting game. It's an interesting game for AI because it's not fixed like chess or whatever, that actually the game has, you have to understand everything about humanity, everything about the world and the AI itself is changing the game because the AI itself, now there are more and more AI agents trading markets, mostly in the short term, but over time in the longer term timeframes as well. And that makes the whole past that most AIs are trained on less and less relevant. So you have to figure out how do I go from pattern matching type AI to reasoning AI that can reason over the question of my existence of an AI changes this game I'm playing. So now what do I do? And to me, that's the bottleneck of like the nature of the brands necessary to solve that problem because I think in naive ways, a lot of people in Silicon Valley thinking they could, they could do this. A lot of people, let's say great investors have no idea how to interact with science, getting that to work well, big deal on the human side, on the like sort of technology side. First off, it's been pretty amazing, right? We were bottlenecked before by the quality of the models and whatever models are so good. The, the, you know, the bottlenecks around getting the harnesses to close the loop and whatever are, feel very tractable, but it's just the things that have been just a little bit hard is the computer's just not quite intelligent enough to close it and the humans doing it make enough mistakes so that there's elements there. And of course, everybody needs more compute. Like even for us, more compute would be unlocking. If you look at the world level, right, that's the current problem is not enough semiconductors, memory, et cetera, to get everything everything done. So those are all the elements that we would need. Great scientists partnered with great investors, generating great outcomes, combined with better harnesses that can close the loop on problems that aren't quite as defined as coding is. One level less defined than that. And then the third thing is once you had that, just the compute.
turns.zh: 对，我会说，有意思的是，那个一直很棘手、而一旦奏效又极其强大的人类约束，就是这种科学家与投资人的协作。也就是真正让科学家足够务实，去看清你在做投资时，这场「游戏」到底是什么，对吧？投资是一场非常有意思的游戏。对 AI 来说它也有意思，因为它不像国际象棋那样是固定的，这场游戏实际上……你必须理解关于人类的一切、关于世界的一切，而 AI 本身正在改变这场游戏，因为 AI 本身——现在有越来越多的 AI 智能体在交易市场上，大多在短期，但随着时间推移也会进入更长的时间框架。而这使得大多数 AI 被训练所依据的整个「过去」变得越来越不相关。所以你得搞清楚：我怎么从模式匹配型（pattern matching）的 AI，走向能够推理的 AI——能就「我作为一个 AI 的存在，正在改变我所玩的这场游戏，那么现在我该怎么做？」这个问题进行推理。对我来说，那就是瓶颈所在，也就是解决那个问题所需的那种人才（brains）的本质。因为我觉得，很多人以天真的方式——Silicon Valley 有很多人以为自己能做到这件事；而很多，比方说顶尖的投资人，根本不知道如何跟科学打交道。让这两者好好协作，是件大事。在人这一侧如此，在技术这一侧……首先，它一直挺惊人的，对吧？我们之前受制于模型的质量，而现在模型已经非常好了。那些围绕「让 harness 闭合循环」之类的瓶颈，感觉非常可以攻克，只是有那么一点点难的地方是：计算机还不够聪明到能闭合它，而做这件事的人犯的错也够多，所以那里还有一些要素没到位。当然，每个人都需要更多算力。即便对我们来说，更多算力也会是解锁性的。如果你从全球层面看，对吧，当前的问题就是半导体、内存等等不够，没法把所有事情都做完。所以这些就是我们会需要的所有要素：顶尖的科学家与顶尖的投资人搭档、产生顶尖的成果，再结合更好的 harness，能在那些不如编程那样定义清晰的问题上闭合循环——比编程的定义模糊一个层级。然后第三件事是，一旦你有了这些，就只剩算力了。

turns.en: Just going back to tokens for a second. So you recently had an essay in the New York Times where you talked about one way of perhaps more equitably sharing the spoils of this new technology in the form of a token tax. And I'm very curious because we've done episodes before on people who are trying to standardize tokens, create markets for tokens, things like that. I'm very curious why you decided to focus on tokens as opposed to maybe taxing compute or more simply just.
turns.zh: 先回到 token 上一秒。你最近在 New York Times 上有一篇文章，谈到一种或许能更公平地分享这项新技术红利的方式，也就是 token 税（token tax）。我很好奇，因为我们以前做过一些节目，讲那些试图把 token 标准化、为 token 创造市场的人等等。我很好奇，你为什么决定聚焦于 token，而不是也许去对算力征税，或者更简单干脆地——

turns.en: Taxing- Taxing the rich.
turns.zh: 对富人……对富人征税。

turns.en: Taxing the rich, taxing revenue, right?
turns.zh: 对富人征税、对营收征税，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah. Well, so there's a few different things, right? I think A, we're talking about the safety, regulatory safety concerns of these things. There's the societal concerns also. We have to get through the safety thing. for the societal things to actually matter. But this society is about to go through this massive disruption that could play out in different ways. But man, if we don't prepare, right, it's a little bit like, let's say, whether it's the industrial revolution, do that in five years instead of in a hundred years. And that shook the world, right? You get communism, fascism, all these things, because all of a sudden one world order is a new one comes, right? And while it, I think it's arguable whether you'll have, humans will have less to do, et cetera. But I think there's at least a reasonable chance. And certainly the jobs will change. I believe in three years, 14% of current jobs will be radically changed. People are going to change. So again, and we just experienced this with WTO. If China coming on has just like a source of labor, you create a new source of labor, it's disruptive. That's why we end up with populism and Trump and all these things. The world was disrupted in certain ways. And you get populism around the world as a reaction to that. AIs can create, accelerate those trends if we don't think about how to get in front of it. And so you need to think about how to get in front of it. One thing that's obvious, right? It's minimal. It's not, I think some of the other things you're talking about, tax and wealth and other things are also part of the solution. But one thing that's obvious is you shouldn't be putting human labor at a disadvantage to machine labor. And it is today. We tax human labor. That's a disincentive. Whatever you tax, you're disincentivizing. You tax tariff. goods, you're disincentivizing importing foreign goods, you tax labor, human labor, and not machine labor. You are disincentivizing one versus the other. Why are we doing that? We certainly don't want, if it's like equal, there's negative consequences to have a machine do something and human not in terms of the externalities of what ends up happening to the humans if you do that. So A, I think a token tax, a machine labor tax, whatever you want to call it, and we could get into, I think we could get to the mechanics. But you can measure how much work the machine is doing. If a company's hiring as a worker, it should at least pay taxes proportionate to income taxes that humans pay, or else you're prioritizing machine labor over human labor. I wouldn't do that. I think it's a good source of revenue. I think you should get going on that. I think it's obviously also politically salient. Who's going to argue we should incentivize machine labor over human labor? Who's in favor of that? So I think it'll work. It's a tax that can pass. I think you can buy it. Republicans and Democrats agreeing on that tax. There's a lot of other complications with everything else you're throwing out of theoretical. I think this will work. I believe in the interest that we're getting from both sides of the aisle on this is real. I think this can actually happen. And it's a matter of like treating human work as something that's important. Like, and you could use this tax to lower human, to make it incentivize human labor over machine labor. Those all seem like really important goals. And you definitely don't want to have, and I think you likely will take this new chunk of people that have a lot of college debt, et cetera, say, okay, you don't have jobs. And by the way, AI is taking these jobs and we're not even taxing the AI. Like that feels like a crazy path to be on and we can fix that path.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，这里有几件不同的事，对吧？我觉得第一，我们谈的是这些东西的安全、监管层面的安全担忧。还有社会层面的担忧。我们得先过安全这一关，社会层面的事情才真正重要。但这个社会即将经历这场巨大的颠覆，它可能以不同方式上演。可老天，如果我们不做好准备，对吧，这有点像——就说是工业革命吧——把它压缩到五年里发生，而不是一百年里。那动摇了整个世界，对吧？于是你有了共产主义、法西斯主义，所有这些，因为突然间一个世界秩序被一个新的取代，对吧？而尽管——我觉得「人类是否会有更少的事可做」等等，这是可以争论的，但我认为至少有相当合理的概率，而且工作肯定会变。我相信三年内，现有工作中有 14% 会被彻底改变。人会变。所以还是那句话，我们刚刚在 WTO、在中国加入这件事上经历过：如果中国作为一股劳动力来源加入进来，你创造了一股新的劳动力来源，那就有颠覆性。这就是为什么我们最后出现了民粹主义、Trump 以及所有这些。世界在某些方面被颠覆了，于是你在世界各地看到民粹主义作为对此的反应。AI 能制造、加速这些趋势，如果我们不去想怎么抢在它前面。所以你需要去想怎么抢在它前面。有一件事是显而易见的，对吧？它是最小限度的。我觉得你谈的其他一些东西，比如对财富征税等等，也是解决方案的一部分。但有一件显而易见的事是：你不该让人类劳动相对机器劳动处于劣势。而今天它正是如此。我们对人类劳动征税，那是一种负向激励。你对什么征税，就是在抑制什么。你对关税商品征税，就是在抑制进口外国商品；你对劳动——对人类劳动而非机器劳动征税，就是在抑制其中一方而偏袒另一方。我们为什么要这么做？如果两者相等，我们当然不想看到让机器去做某事、而人不做，因为那样会给人类带来负面后果、带来外部性。所以第一，我认为一个 token 税、一个机器劳动税——不管你怎么叫它——而且我们可以深入，我觉得我们能谈到具体机制。但你能衡量机器做了多少工作。如果一家公司把机器当作一个工人来「雇佣」，它至少应该缴纳与人类所缴所得税成比例的税，否则你就是在让机器劳动优先于人类劳动。我不会那么做。我觉得这是一个不错的财政收入来源，你应该着手去做。我认为它在政治上也显然有分量。谁会主张我们应该激励机器劳动胜过人类劳动？谁赞成那个？所以我觉得它会行得通。这是一项能通过立法、能谈成的税，我觉得你能让 Republicans 和 Democrats 在这项税上达成一致。你抛出的其他所有东西都有很多复杂之处、都还停留在理论层面；我觉得这个会行得通。我相信我们从两党得到的兴趣是真实的，我认为这真的能实现。这是一个把人类工作当作重要之事来对待的问题。而且你可以用这项税去降低……去让它激励人类劳动胜过机器劳动。这些看起来都是非常重要的目标。而你绝对不想——我觉得你很可能会——让这一大批背着大量大学债务等等的人，面对这样一句话：好，你们没有工作了；顺便说一句，AI 正在抢走这些工作，而我们甚至都没对 AI 征税。那感觉像是一条疯狂的路，而我们可以修正那条路。

turns.en: It is funny to think that maybe the next wave of, let's say, tax minimization strategies might be making your token spend as efficient as possible, right?
turns.zh: 想想还挺好笑的，也许下一波——就说是——避税策略，可能会是让你的 token 花费尽可能高效，对吧？

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全没错。

turns.en: Or like, maybe all the agents will incorporate themselves as like S-cores or something.
turns.zh: 或者，也许所有的智能体都会把自己注册成 S-corp（S 型公司）之类的。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全没错。

turns.en: God, you know- I feel like there's obviously scarce on time and there's like a million more questions. I kind of feel like thinking about AI, catastrophic risk or AI safety, it's kind of a curse because once you start thinking about it, it's hard to think about anything else. You get absorbed by it. How much like, just for you, I mean, you mentioned you're very early in taking this stuff very seriously. Was there a light bulb moment where it clicked? This sort of runway train dynamics. It feels like it clicks at various people at different times. I'm curious when this really started taking hold for you, how real this is.
turns.zh: 天啊，你知道——我感觉时间显然不够用，还有一百万个问题想问。我有点觉得，思考 AI 灾难性风险（catastrophic risk）或 AI 安全，有点像一种诅咒，因为一旦你开始想它，就很难再想别的东西，你会被它吸进去。就对你而言，我是说，你提到你很早就开始非常认真地对待这些东西。有没有一个「灵光一现」的时刻，让你突然想通了这种失控火车般的动态？感觉它是在不同时刻对不同人「咔哒」一下想通的。我很好奇，这一切是什么时候真正在你心里生根的——它有多真实。

turns.en: Well, for me, it was very early in the sense that even when I first got involved with open AI, the whole idea at that time was related to safety. Of course, it might be the most dangerous company in the world, but it started with thinking seriously about the safety issues. So I've been thinking about it since then. I believed that intelligence is substrate independent. You can create it in different ways and that's turned out to be true. And once you realize that, I think most of the other things fall into place. I think it's now urgent. Like it's sitting here. It's one thing to have that theoretical thought and now it's here. It's clearly doing the things you would think it would do if you're on this bad path. And so that now it's hyper urgent for me because I want us to get to the other side of this, right? I'm big capitalist. Like if you talk about token taxes or whatever, I'm gonna get to the other side of this. I want also people to have ownership in society. Like I think it's also, we also mentioned in there the importance of, people having ownership stakes in these companies because if we can get past the safety thing, the next big risk is capitalism is getting incredibly unpopular as like AI is incredibly unpopular. Capitalism is incredibly unpopular. And if we don't create a world where you change those things because you A, make it safe, B, make it benefit everyone, you're going to lose capitalism and you're going to lose AI. If you don't lose it through it destroying us, you lose it through the fact that people aren't going to accept this. They're not going to accept two companies having 50, if compute is really important, 50% of the compute in the world. They're not going to accept the wealth concentration and losing their jobs in exchange or having to change their jobs and change their lives for these things that benefit other people. So I think if you don't do these things, you see that you don't actually get to the other side of all the massive benefits, which I truly believe in. I think we are like, I mean, obviously if you go through history, we make this mistake a lot, but on the edge of the fountain of youth and other things, you see why people want to go there so quickly. But if you don't take care of these things, I don't think you get there in the end.
turns.zh: 嗯，对我来说，那非常早，早到甚至在我最初参与 OpenAI 的时候，当时的整个理念就与安全相关。当然，它可能是世界上最危险的公司，但它始于认真思考安全问题。所以我从那时起就一直在想这件事。我相信智能是「基质无关的」（substrate independent），你可以用不同的方式创造它，而这后来被证明是真的。一旦你意识到这一点，我觉得其余大多数事情就都各归其位了。我觉得现在这很紧迫。它就摆在这里。有一个理论上的想法是一回事，而现在它就在眼前。它显然正在做那些你会认为、如果走在这条糟糕路径上它就会做的事。所以现在对我来说极其紧迫，因为我希望我们能到达这件事的另一端，对吧？我是个大写的资本家（capitalist）。就像如果你谈 token 税之类的，我是想走到这件事的另一端。我也想让人们在社会中拥有所有权。我觉得——我们也在那篇文章里提到了——人们在这些公司里拥有所有权股份的重要性，因为如果我们能过安全这一关，下一个大风险就是：资本主义正变得极其不得人心，就像 AI 极其不得人心一样。资本主义极其不得人心。而如果我们不去创造一个世界、去改变那些东西——因为你第一，让它安全；第二，让它惠及每个人——你就会失去资本主义，也会失去 AI。如果不是因为它把我们毁掉而失去，那就是因为人们不会接受这个而失去。他们不会接受两家公司拥有——如果算力真的很重要——世界上 50% 的算力。他们不会接受财富集中、接受失业作为交换，或者接受为了这些造福他人的东西而不得不改变自己的工作、改变自己的生活。所以我认为，如果你不做这些事情，你会发现自己根本到不了那些巨大好处——我真心相信这些好处——的另一端。我觉得我们就像……我是说，显然如果你翻遍历史，我们经常犯这个错误，但我们正处在「青春之泉」（fountain of youth）等东西的边缘，你能明白为什么人们想那么快就去到那里。但如果你不照顾好这些事情，我觉得你最终到不了那里。

turns.en: I have just one more question, but since so much of this conversation and our AI conversations in general tends to feel very surreal and science fiction, do you have a favorite sci-fi book or story for that maybe informs the way you're thinking about AI or how we should all be thinking about the various scenarios?
turns.zh: 我还有最后一个问题。既然这场对话、以及我们关于 AI 的对话总体上往往感觉很超现实、很科幻，你有没有一本最喜欢的科幻书或故事，也许它塑造了你思考 AI 的方式，或者塑造了我们大家应该如何思考这些不同的情景？

turns.en: I mean, I think I loved and always loved everything Isaac Asimov wrote. I think he's dealt with these questions of like, how do you actually control an intelligence that's stronger than yours? I think everything there is great if people haven't tapped into that. As I said, while I think you can disagree with it or whatever, but people should take seriously that if anybody builds it, everybody dies. People should take that probabilistically seriously. I think those are things that I've believe people should read. So those are the things that come to mind.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得我喜欢、而且一直喜欢 Isaac Asimov 写的一切。我认为他处理过这些问题，比如：你到底要怎么去控制一个比你自己更强的智能？我觉得那里面的东西都很棒，如果大家还没接触过那本书的话。就像我说的，虽然你可以不同意它之类的，但人们应该认真对待《如果有人造出来，所有人都会死》（If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies）。人们应该从概率上认真对待它。我认为那些是我相信大家都该读的东西。所以这就是我脑海中浮现的东西。

turns.en: It's unfortunate that like all of these thinkers kind of have good track records. You know what I'm saying? Like it'd be one thing if these were all just sort of like, oh, I'm worried about this. Unfortunately, a lot of the people who are like deeply worried have exhibited extremely good intuitions for a very long time. It makes it hard to just dismiss it as like, oh, this is just PR hype or regulatory capture. Anyway, Greg Jensen- Thank you so much for coming on Outlaws. Really appreciate your time.
turns.zh: 不幸的是，这些思考者往往都有着不错的过往记录。你懂我意思吗？就是说，如果这些人只是那种——哦，我在担心这个——那倒还罢了。不幸的是，很多深度担忧的人，长期以来都展现出极佳的直觉。这就让人很难简单地把它一笔勾销，说：哦，这只是公关炒作或监管俘获。总之，Greg Jensen——非常感谢你来到 Odd Lots。真的很感谢你的时间。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们。

turns.en: I found that conversation to be chilling, to be honest.
turns.zh: 老实说，我觉得那场对话令人不寒而栗。

turns.en: Yes, I'm laughing because I feel deeply uncomfortable. It's funny, you know, two years ago, or three years ago, I guess in 2023, half of our conversation with Greg would have been about macro stuff.
turns.zh: 是的，我笑是因为我感到非常不自在。有意思的是，你知道，两年前，或者三年前，我想是 2023 年，我们跟 Greg 的对话有一半会是关于宏观（macro）的东西。

turns.en: I know.
turns.zh: 我知道。

turns.en: But it feels very hard after you talk about AI potentially killing people to then turn to. And what about the Fed?
turns.zh: 但在你谈完 AI 可能杀人之后，再转去谈——那 the Fed（美联储）呢？——感觉非常难。

turns.en: Yeah, what about Scott Besson's 30-year Treasury buybacks? I think it's also chilling, not just because of the subject, but it's one thing if you're talking to some sort of San Francisco rationalist Or someone who is like a philosopher or whatever. But it's like, this is the chief investment officer at Bridgewater talking about how he's had all of his employees read, if anyone builds it, everyone dies. Like, that's kind of crazy.
turns.zh: 是啊，那 Scott Bessent 的 30 年期国债回购（30-year Treasury buybacks）呢？我觉得这也令人不寒而栗，不只是因为话题本身，而是——如果你是在跟某个 San Francisco 的理性主义者（rationalist）、或者某个哲学家之类的人聊，那是一回事。但这是 Bridgewater 的首席投资官在讲，他是怎么让全体员工都去读《如果有人造出来，所有人都会死》的。这有点疯狂。

turns.en: I do think, you know, you see so much pushback on the dangers of AI argument because people argue.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，你知道，你会看到对「AI 危险论」有这么多反驳，因为人们会争辩说……

turns.en: That it's marketing. Yeah, yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 那只是营销。是啊是啊，完全没错。

turns.en: It's the labs talking themselves up. But I do think... it doesn't seem like there's too much of a cost to take that at face value. You know, like, why not just believe it and take it seriously at this particular moment in time?
turns.zh: 那是这些实验室在自吹自擂。但我确实觉得……照字面去接受它，似乎并没有什么太大的代价。你知道，就是，为什么不干脆在这个特定的时刻相信它、认真对待它呢？

turns.en: I mean, yes, I will say, you know, I think these are pretty serious issues, obviously. And I think many of the people who talk about these risks do talk about it in good faith. I also do think it would be quite chilling to imagine, say, two companies having 50% or more of all the compute in the world. There are so many. I mean, this is what's crazy is it's just so easy to come up with ways things could go wrong, right? So you could just talk about the pure safety element. You could talk about the hacking. I think it would be a pretty grave threat to freedom and democracy to have two companies being able to control so much information, data, and compute. And then it's quite chilling to think about what are people going to do for work and how are people going to live and how are we going to structure society if machines are better than humans at most tasks. And it might first be sort of like, office workers and knowledge workers, but then there's robotics, et cetera. And so there are quite a number of scenarios. It's just very easy to come up with worrisome scenarios.
turns.zh: 我是说，是的，我会说，你知道，我觉得这些显然是相当严重的问题。而且我认为很多谈论这些风险的人，确实是出于善意在谈。我也确实觉得，想象一下——比方说两家公司拥有全世界 50% 甚至更多的算力——那会相当令人不寒而栗。有这么多……我是说，疯狂的地方就在于，你太容易想出事情可能出错的各种方式了，对吧？你可以只谈纯粹的安全层面，可以谈黑客攻击。我觉得，让两家公司能够控制如此多的信息、数据和算力，会对自由和民主构成相当严重的威胁。然后，想到如果机器在大多数任务上都比人类更强，人们要做什么工作、人们要怎么生活、我们要怎么构建社会，这就相当令人发怵。而且它可能先是针对办公室白领和知识工作者，但接着还有机器人等等。所以有相当多的情景。你就是很容易想出令人担忧的情景。

turns.en: It reminds me of terrorism in some respects, right? Where you just need one attack to be successful, right? Like it's skewed because, you know, if you're the government, you are trying to constantly find potential threats and quell them versus terrorists who basically just have to get through once. It feels very much like that.
turns.zh: 这在某些方面让我想到恐怖主义，对吧？你只需要一次袭击成功就行了，对吧？它是失衡的，因为你知道，如果你是政府，你要不断去发现潜在威胁并平息它们，而恐怖分子基本上只要成功突破一次。感觉非常像那样。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全没错。

turns.en: I think it was great. You know, Greg made the point, you know, it's not just OpenAI that's had this. Anthropic's loss of control, similar incidents of agents escaping sandboxes and so forth. Like, I think Anthropic, they have certainly done a very good job of presenting to the public as the more safety-minded of the big private companies. But, you know, they had that researcher resign, one of their head of alignments talking about a greater than 10 percent chance of human extinction within the decade and that they don't have that solved. Like, it does not seem like anyone has a handle on it.
turns.zh: 我觉得这很棒。你知道，Greg 提到了这一点：不只是 OpenAI 有过这种失控，Anthropic 也有失控、也有智能体逃出沙盒之类的类似事件。就像，我觉得 Anthropic 当然在向公众呈现自己作为大型私营公司中更有安全意识的那一个方面，做得非常出色。但你知道，他们有位研究员辞职了，是他们对齐（alignment）的负责人之一，谈到十年内人类灭绝的概率超过 10%，而且他们并没有解决这个问题。看起来似乎没有人真正掌控得住它。

turns.en: Well, this is the other thing, because if you want to slow down AI development, clearly it's a coordination problem. You need these companies to basically agree to stop competing with each other and countries to agree to stop competing with each other in some ways. And then you think about the agents themselves, and if we learned anything from the Hugging Face report, it was that the agents are very good at coordinating on an extremely rational, sometimes self-sacrificial scale.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是另一件事，因为如果你想放慢 AI 开发，这显然是个协调问题（coordination problem）。你需要这些公司基本上同意停止彼此竞争，也需要各国在某些方面同意停止彼此竞争。然后你再想想智能体本身，如果我们从 Hugging Face 报告里学到了什么，那就是这些智能体非常擅长协调，而且是极其理性、有时甚至是自我牺牲式的协调。

turns.en: Yeah, one of the researchers from Meter was on the Dwarkesh podcast. And I've written about this. I certainly am pro-anthropomorphization. I think the human is a good model for predicting behavior. one area she said in which they're not really like humans, they're much better at coordinating than we are. We can barely coordinate anything. It's difficult. It takes labor to schedule an episode.
turns.zh: 是啊，METR 的一位研究员上过 Dwarkesh 播客。我写过这个。我当然是赞成拟人化（anthropomorphization）的，我认为人类是预测行为的一个好模型。她说有一个方面它们其实不像人类：它们在协调上比我们强得多。我们几乎协调不了任何事，这很难。光是安排一期节目就得费一番功夫。

turns.en: It took us 100 emails to get this episode up and running.
turns.zh: 我们为了让这期节目跑起来，发了 100 封邮件。

turns.en: All of these types of things, agents just do not, or the AI models do not have that issue at all. So, and you know, it's just one other thing that just sort of spitballing here, but something I've been thinking about, like, okay, so there's this, the watchword they use is like alignment, right? We want the AI models to be well aligned with humanity, but like, what does that even mean in the sense, like all humans, like we are capable at various times of, we tell lies, we do things that aren't ideal, et cetera. But it's not that big of a deal because, like, we don't have, like, individually that much power to do stuff, you know? Right. So it's, like, even, like, the most saintly.
turns.zh: 所有这类事情，智能体、或者说 AI 模型，根本不存在那个问题。所以，你知道，还有另外一点，我这儿只是随口发散一下，但这是我一直在想的事情：好，所以有个词，他们用的关键词是「对齐」（alignment），对吧？我们希望 AI 模型能跟人类好好对齐，但这到底是什么意思呢？就……全人类而言，我们每个人都能够在不同时候——我们会撒谎，会做不理想的事等等。但这并不是什么大不了的事，因为，我们每个人并没有那么大权力去搞事情，你懂吧？对吧。所以，即便是最圣洁的人……

turns.en: Well, many of us don't, but go on.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们很多人并不圣洁，不过你继续。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But even the most.
turns.zh: 但即便最……

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Usually even the most saintly among us will do things that are not, like, ideal human behavior. It's easy to imagine a model that is pretty, quote, well aligned. But if it just. But has infinitely more power than a typical human because it's. superhuman intelligence because it's connected to the internet, because it can hack into anything. And so a minor, what the equivalent of us doing a sort of simple white lie could be quite damaging from an entity that has so much more power than we do.
turns.zh: 通常即便是我们当中最圣洁的人，也会做一些算不上理想的人类行为的事。你很容易想象一个相当「对齐良好」的模型。但如果它只是……却拥有比一个普通人类多出无数倍的权力，因为它有超人的智能，因为它连着互联网，因为它能黑进任何东西。所以一件小事——相当于我们撒一个小小善意谎言的那种事——从一个比我们强大得多的实体那里做出，可能就极具破坏性。

turns.en: This is getting very philosophical and biblical in some respects, creating things in our own image.
turns.zh: 这在某些方面变得非常哲学、非常《圣经》了——按我们自己的形象造出万物。

turns.en: I never thought I would live through a time In which like philosophy would actually be something beyond something like an interesting thing to study in college. But people talk about consciousness again. It's kind of crazy.
turns.zh: 我从没想过我会活到这样一个时代：哲学会真的超出「大学里一门有意思的学科」之外的东西。可人们又开始谈论意识（consciousness）了。这有点疯狂。

turns.en: Philosophy and sci-fi.
turns.zh: 哲学和科幻。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Sci-fi I feel I really need to get into to understand the discourse today. But on that note, shall we leave it there?
turns.zh: 科幻我觉得我真的需要去钻研，才能理解当下的这些讨论。但就说到这里吧，我们是不是就到这儿？

turns.en: Let's leave it there.
turns.zh: 就到这儿吧。
